Former ambassador on NATO's meeting in Ukraine and the ongoing war Military representatives from all 32 NATO member states met in Kyiv. NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with Kurt Volker, former U.S. ambassador to NATO, about the meeting and the ongoing war.
Former ambassador on NATO's meeting in Ukraine and the ongoing war
Former ambassador on NATO's meeting in Ukraine and the ongoing war
< iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5993774/nx-s1-9956490" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Military representatives from all 32 NATO member states met in Kyiv. NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with Kurt Volker, former U.S. ambassador to NATO, about the meeting and the ongoing war.
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: Military representatives from all 32 NATO nations met this week, and what is notable is where they met - Kyiv, Ukraine. They seem to be there to learn. Kurt Volker is following all this. He's a former U.S. ambassador to NATO and former representative to Ukraine in the first Trump administration. Welcome back. KURT VOLKER: Thank you very much, Steve. Good to be with you. INSKEEP: What are the NATO members learning? VOLKER: Well, I think the first thing they want to get a look at firsthand is the air defense situation for Kyiv and other cities during the winter. Russia has really stepped up its air raids against Ukraine to try to knock out the electricity grid and other heating and things during the winter. And I think they want to get a look firsthand how Ukraine is doing, how prepared they are for the winter, what kind of things NATO countries might need to do. INSKEEP: OK. That makes sense because we've seen these massive, much more constant air attacks on Kyiv, for example, and concerns about how they would get through the winter. Do the NATO allies have the capacity to help Ukraine with that? VOLKER: They do. Obviously, the best system in the world is the Patriot system that we have provided in the past and allies have bought for Ukraine, but they're in very short supply. But there are other types as well that NATO allies can provide to help with air defense. The Germans, the French, Swedes, all have different variations of this. And then the other thing that the NATO representatives want to do is to get a look firsthand at what Ukraine is doing on its own. They now have some of the best in the world capabilities when it comes to drones, counter-drones and electronic warfare. And it's much more efficient the way the Ukrainians are taking out drones that are incoming than the way NATO countries have done it. So we have something to learn from the Ukrainians in this too. INSKEEP: This is amazing. So you're telling me we're in this world of asymmetric warfare where maybe the people with the biggest and most expensive weapons don't win. I guess this is an important lesson for the United States to learn, since the United States is the country with the biggest and most expensive weapons. They're not always the best ones? VOLKER: Well, they can be the best, but they're also very expensive. And when you have someone that can send thousands of drones per night - and maybe the drones cost $30,000 - you're going to knock that down with a million-dollar interceptor missile? You can't keep doing that repeatedly. So we've got to learn some of these low-cost and high-volume ways to take these things out the way the Ukrainians have done. INSKEEP: Is this the lesson of the Iran where - war, where the United States has spent billions against armed forces that seem to be able to respond very cheaply? VOLKER: Yes, exactly. And in fact, the drones that the Iranians have used against targets in the Middle East - both U.S. bases and our Gulf allies - are the very same drones that Russia has been using against Ukraine for a long time. And so the Ukrainians have had a lot of time and experience now to figure out how to deal with these. The U.S. was using a large number of Patriot missiles to take down these very same things. That's why we now have a global shortage of Patriots - because we were using them with such volume compared to what we could have been doing if we had better lower-cost systems at hand. INSKEEP: I think you said something that is very relevant here because you said Ukraine is leading the world in drones - or near leading the world in drones - but also counter-drones. VOLKER: Yes. INSKEEP: So this is a category of defensive drone? That's what the U.S. and others need to learn about? VOLKER: Well, it's not - they do have defensive drones - the drones that take out drones - but they also have lower-cost systems that are targeted more at the low-cost drones that come in. So for example, you have a regular propeller-driven drone. You don't want to use an anti-aircraft or an antimissile missile to take that out. You can do that with a ground-based firing system that is lower tech, lower cost, but effective. The jet-powered ones are harder, but they're now learning ways to take those out too. INSKEEP: Just very briefly, you mentioned electronic warfare. What do you mean by that in this context? VOLKER: It - it's rerouting where the incoming missile or the incoming drone is supposed to go. By confusing the signals, it ends up not hitting the target, in some cases just crashing into the ground or into a river. The most famous one of these is called Lima. They reprogram the incoming missile to think its target is Lima, Peru... INSKEEP: Wow (laughter). VOLKER: ...Which is too far away to hit, so it crashes. INSKEEP: OK. Wow. Kurt Volker, former U.S. ambassador to NATO. Thanks for your insights. Appreciate it. VOLKER: My pleasure. Thanks.

A sign displays the prices of unleaded gasoline and diesel fuel as a driver refuels a vehicle at a G&M gas station in Torrance, California, US, on September 28, 2026.
Oil prices climbed Thursday on continued worries about global supply following a record number of tanker attacks that sent crossings through the Strait of Hormuz to a two-month low.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, rose more than 5% at one point before pulling back to trade 4.8% higher at $105 a barrel at 8.30 a.m. ET . West Texas Intermediate, the US benchmark, increased by a similar margin to $92.48 a barrel.
Just seven tankers transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, less than half the seven-day average and the lowest number since July 23, preliminary data from Kpler showed. These figures are at times revised higher after ships have moved through the strait, as many switch off their identification systems to try to avoid detection.
Despite the rising number of so-called “dark” transits, there have been a record number of attacks on commercial vessels, with 10 tankers struck in the strait between September 28 and October 4, well above the previous weekly high of six, Kpler said in a report Thursday.
The rise in attacks comes even as more crude has been flowing out of the Gulf , highlighting the ongoing risks to crew and cargoes. In the latest attack Wednesday, a tanker reported being struck by “multiple projectiles,” causing casualties, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said.
“There is a clear tug-of-war at the moment between improving supply from the region and lingering threats to supply,” commodities strategists at ING, a bank, wrote in a note Wednesday. “The only way to see prices trade sustainably lower is for lingering risks to be addressed,” they added.
Upward pressure on oil prices also came from concerns about further supply losses as Hurricane Isais heads towards America’s refining hub on the Gulf Coast. Oil majors Shell and Chevron said they would curtail production in the region and evacuate nonessential personnel.
The Shell Norco petroleum refinery and the Valero St. Charles oil refinery are seen in Norco, Louisiana, on April 2, 2026.
A major hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
Rising oil prices were accompanied by an increase in European natural gas and diesel prices, fanning inflation fears and contributing to a renewed selloff in European bonds given the continent’s reliance on imported energy.
European benchmark natural gas prices neared their recent high from mid-September earlier on Thursday before pulling back. ICE Gasoil Futures, a benchmark for European diesel prices, closed 6% higher on Wednesday after the International Energy Agency said member governments would not add to the 400 million barrels of oil they agreed to release in March.
To date, roughly 325 million barrels of oil have been released, with approximately 100 million more barrels still to be brought to the market, the IEA said in a statement Wednesday, pledging to “accelerate” those releases. Those 100 million barrels would include the diesel release that G7 countries agreed to last week .
“IEA Member governments still have significant levels of publicly held emergency oil stocks – equivalent to around 1.1 billion barrels, including over 200 million barrels of diesel,” the Paris-based energy body said.
“The IEA stands ready to release more of these stocks to the market if and when required.”
Average US diesel prices at gas stations were slightly lower on Thursday than the day before, at $6.28 a gallon. Average US regular gasoline prices were flat on the previous day at $4.36 a gallon, according to AAA data.

items.summary: Fed’s Waller sees additional rate hikes to get inflation down faster  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
Fed's Waller sees additional rate hikes to get inflation down faster
Federal Reserve Governor Chris Waller said in a speech Thursday that he expects the Fed will need to enact more interest rate hikes to bring down inflation faster if economic data comes in as he expects.
"If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal," Waller said at the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye İstanbul Economic Forum. "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
Waller noted that a convergence of factors has gelled into persistent inflationary forces, including hopes for a quick ending to the Middle East conflict and warnings that low inventories and damaged infrastructure could keep oil prices high through 2027. He also pointed out that the artificial intelligence build-out has significantly driven up high-tech consumer prices , and projections of its size have ballooned. Additionally, he said, continuing trade conflicts threaten new tariffs that could put upward pressure on inflation yet again.
"When the first inflation reading for August came in hot just before the FOMC's September meeting, it was impossible to deny that inflation was still too high and not making sufficient progress toward our target," Waller said.
Waller sees economic activity strengthening in the second half of this year, and says he's "not greatly concerned" that higher interest rates threaten to markedly slow down the economy.
"But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation."
He noted that he sees the economy in roughly the same place as it was at the time of the Fed's policy meeting in mid-September.
"Overall, the new data reinforce my view that the labor market is stable and inflation is too high," he said. "For at least the near term, policy will be focused on the inflation side of our mandate."
Waller also made a point of sharing how he believes the Fed should communicate its interest rate expectations . He doesn't think choosing to say nothing or offering a strong indication of what the Fed will do is how the central bank should communicate. Rather, he believes an in-between approach of signaling the amount of rate hikes over some time interval, while not saying what the pace of hikes will be or how large they will be, would offer flexibility, while keeping the public informed.
"We could emphasize that the course of monetary policy is not predetermined and will depend on incoming data," he said.
"Policymakers could signal where they are likely headed while acknowledging that there is no fixed final destination — except for the achievement of price stability and maximum employment."

Fed's Musalem says tighter monetary policy needed to lower inflation
Alberto Musalem, President and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, speaks to the Economic Club of New York, in New York City, U.S., February 20, 2025. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid · Reuters
NEW YORK, Oct 8 (Reuters) - St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem said on Thursday the US central bank will need to hike interest rates again to bring inflation back to ‌its 2% target, although he declined to say what policymakers should do at their meeting later this month.
"To ‌bring inflation back to target in a timely manner, more monetary policy firming will be required," Musalem said at an event held by Bloomberg in ​New York.
"If a timely manner is something like 18 months, that kind of suggests that rates ought to be going up further in an appropriate period of time in the next six to nine months," he said.
Musalem, who is not a voting member of the central bank's rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee this year, demurred when asked if the Fed should raise rates at the ‌October 27-28 meeting.
"I go into every meeting ⁠with a very open mind, and I haven't prejudged what the outcome of that meeting is going to be, or what I'm going to do at that meeting," Musalem said, adding that ⁠the general direction of "inflation requires us to be thinking of further policy firming here."
Traders broadly expect the Fed will hold its policy rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range at the meeting in October. The Fed hiked rates at its September 15-16 meeting in an effort to ​bring ​high levels of inflation back to its target.
Policymakers at that meeting ​also penciled in another rate hike by the end ‌of this year. Traders had been putting strong odds on an October rate hike until New York Fed President John Williams said last week that there is no urgency to act while the Fed weighs incoming data. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson followed up by saying he saw no imminent need to raise rates.
The Fed is now expected to deliver its next rate hike in December.
In his remarks, Musalem said inflation is the economy's primary problem amid strong growth and ‌a stable job market. He said the Fed can likely lower inflation ​without denting hiring, and that getting inflation back to the 2% goal ​would be broadly helpful.
Musalem also noted that even with ​the notable rise in bond yields, "financial conditions remain accommodative and supportive of economic growth."
He said the ‌rise in yields does not signal investors are ​losing confidence in the Fed. Instead, ​yields are up on expectations that real rates will go up in a strong economy marked by a lot of competition for capital. Strong investment in the tech sector and large government borrowing needs are helping to keep ​yields up, he said.
"The US federal government ‌has been on an unsustainable fiscal path now for the better part of two decades," Musalem said, adding ​that "the risk is there" that heavy levels of government borrowing could create problems for the economy.

items.title: Trump’s pledge not to strike Iran before midterms fails to soothe oil markets - NBC News
items.summary: Trump’s pledge not to strike Iran before midterms fails to soothe oil markets  NBC News
items.content:
Diesel prices have soared, spurred on by recent escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war. Joe Raedle / Getty
Oct. 8, 2026, 8:15 AM EDT  /  Updated   Oct. 8, 2026, 4:19 PM EDT
President Donald Trump’s surprise pledge that the United States would not resume airstrikes against Iran before the midterm elections failed to reverse a sharp jump in oil prices Thursday.
“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote on his social media site, adding that the U.S. was having “productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Trump’s statements have been a significant driver of daily moves in the oil market since the start of the war with Iran in February. But on Thursday, after a brief price dip, oil markets largely shrugged off the president’s announcement.
After rising as high as almost $106 per barrel, Brent crude oil closed at $104.28, a rise of 4%. U.S. crude oil also ended the trading session up 3.6% at $91.49, after earlier jumping to nearly $93.
Other critical energy prices also looked past Trump’s post. Benchmark diesel futures spiked 6% in European trading. Heating oil, a proxy for jet fuel, rose more than 5%.
In addition to the elevated Iran risk, oil prices Thursday reflected traders’ concerns about reports of Iranian proxy attacks in Saudi Arabia.
Hurricane Isaias also figured into the price of oil. Major oil companies with rigs in the Gulf of Mexico announced that work had been suspended at several locations, and crews evacuated as a precaution.
Trump’s post appeared to be a direct response to reports from outlets, including NBC News , that he was considering strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms.
NBC News and others noted that Trump had not yet made a final decision, however.
Key bond yields also dropped following Trump’s post. The 10-year yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates fell to its lowest level since Friday.
Stocks also faced a day of choppy trading, but ultimately they were largely unaffected by the president’s announcement.
Earlier this year, a post like Thursday’s from Trump would have almost certainly driven major indexes sharply higher.
Instead, the broad S&P 500 closed down 0.5% Thursday and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.2%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium-sized companies, closed flat.
News from the tech sector that raised questions about OpenAI’s revenue also helped drag stocks lower.
More Republican candidates break with Trump on key issues
Trump’s decision could have been motivated by any number of factors. But with the midterm elections less than a month out and early voting underway, any substantial action by the Trump White House would likely have at least some impact on voter attitudes.
They could also risk raising oil prices even higher.
For months, Iranian attacks on commercial shipping have reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery for global oil supplies, to just a fraction of prewar levels.
From Sept. 28 through Oct. 4, daily traffic in the strait averaged fewer than 23 ships a day, according to data from MarineTraffic. Before the war, hundreds of ships per day passed through the waterway delivering crude oil and related products to global markets.
Oil and commodities market experts have repeatedly warned that any escalation in the fighting in Iran will cause oil prices to trend even higher.
“The market remains exposed to significant risks,” Bank of America’s head of global commodities, Francisco Blanch, wrote in early September. If skirmishes curbing oil flows continued into the year’s end, he wrote, Brent could trade in a $95-$120 per barrel range.
Trump eases restrictions on 'red-dye' diesel
“Meanwhile, a broader conflict resulting in major energy infrastructure damage may spike prices” as high as $150 per barrel, he added.
The cost to ship crude oil from countries that are not directly impacted by the closure of the strait has also reached new highs, as producers scramble to meet demand.
It now costs $77 million for a crude carrier to move U.S. oil to Asia, according to Bloomberg, which cited data from the Baltic Exchange in London . The average price for the same route in 2025 was just $9.2 million.
The continued elevation of crude oil prices has caused retail gas prices to remain high for U.S. consumers, many of whom have helped make gas prices a major issue in scores of midterm congressional races.
On Thursday, the national average price for regular unleaded gas was $4.36 per gallon. That price is more than 45% higher than when the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28.
Diesel fuel prices have soared even more, spurred on by recent escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war. At $6.28 per gallon Thursday, diesel has risen almost 70% since Feb. 28.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

Italian opposition cries foul as Meloni’s electoral reform passed in secret ballot
Parties vow to challenge law in court, arguing that extra reward for those with 42% of support distorts public representation
A controversial overhaul to electoral law that critics say is aimed at boosting Giorgia Meloni’s chances of clinging on to power in elections next year has been given final approval by the Italian parliament.
Meloni, the Italian prime minister, says the new system, which introduces a fully proportional model, including bonus seats for any coalition that wins the most votes, will bring about greater political stability, while opposition parties argue that it mainly serves the interests of those in power.
The change was passed in a secret ballot in the lower house with 227 MPs voting in favour and 164 against.
There were protests from opposition politicians who held up signs decrying the law as a “scam” and a “con” when the result was announced.
Opposition parties have vowed to challenge the changes in the constitutional court, arguing that the bonus seat element, which would be granted to any coalition that reaches a vote threshold of 42% of the vote, distorts voter representation.
Another contentious requirement of the changes is that parties and alliances would be required lay out their government programme and name their candidate for prime minister well before a general election.
Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy , had made the vote a test for her ruling rightwing coalition, warning MPs from her allies, including Forza Italia and the League, that, if defeated, the government would face a crisis.
While there are tensions within the coalition, which has suffered setbacks in recent months and is under threat from the rise of new far-right rival Roberto Vannacci, leader of Futuro Nazionale, it has put on a show of unity and has stability on its side after becoming Italy’s longest serving government since the second world war in early September. Whereas the broad leftwing alliance, led by the Democratic party, is highly fractious with no clear leader or programme.
Meloni said the victory was a response to those who wanted to see her coalition divided. “Today we respond with action: we are united, cohesive and determined to fulfil the commitments made to citizens,” she wrote on social media.
Elly Schlein, the leader of the Democratic party , said Meloni’s alliance sought to change the electoral system because it feared losing the next general election, which is officially due to be held before October 2027 but could be brought forward to April or May.
According to a recent survey by Ipsos Doxa, the opposition coalition could reach the 42% threshold if it overcame internal divisions and managed to convince two small radical parties to join forces.

items.content:
The new online film mimics some of the style of the real NAZA documentary (above) which uses footage shot from rooftops in Tel Aviv
The new online film mimics some of the style of the real NAZA documentary (above) which uses footage shot from rooftops in Tel Aviv
Embassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civilians
The Israeli government is promoting an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, the award-winning documentary that details Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, in an attempt to counter the real film’s findings.
The real documentary , directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and produced by the Guardian, is in cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries.
The Israeli government has denounced the film and announced plans to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason.
In recent days, Israeli embassies have been promoting a link to a hastily produced online film entitled NAZA: The Real Story. Mimicking some of the style of the real documentary, including the use of anonymised interviews shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv, it is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com.
Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made the new documentary, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians. The film claims that Israel has the “most moral army in the world”.
Another film-maker listed on the website for NAZA: The Real Story is Roi Danino, a candidate for the rightwing Israel First party.
The website domain was registered on 16 September, six days after NAZA’s premiere at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the festival’s history.
Initially, the website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was due to be screened.
“Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza,” it said, distorting the film’s official synopsis by removing the reference to the deaths of Palestinian civilians.
That wording was removed from recent updates of the website, once the video for NAZA: The Real Story had been added to the page.
It now appears as a platform for the rival film, with a counter that implausibly suggests the short film has been watched more than 42m times. (The film’s official YouTube page is listed as having just 30,000 views.)
According to a technical analysis, the discrepancy suggested the viewer counter could have been driven by requests made to the website, by humans or bots, rather than the number of people who actually watched the video. When asked about the source of the 42m claim, Averbuch said he did not know and referred the questions to his tech team.
The Israeli military has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023, in a military campaign that a United Nations commission has described as genocide.
Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham speak onstage at the NAZA premiere at the New York film festival on 26 September. Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty for FLC The 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders in the original film NAZA detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.
The Israeli embassy to the US, which shared the new documentary on its social media, said the ministry of foreign affairs was not involved in producing the film, and that it had intended only to “amplify the message of its creators and expose wider audiences to arguments challenging and dismantling the blood libels and false allegations”.
NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in Gaza
The Israeli government said on Thursday that it was awarding the film-makers with a certificate of appreciation “for their contribution to Israeli public diplomacy”, claiming the production had garnered tens of millions of views.
A Guardian spokesperson said: “We are aware that the Israeli government has been promoting a film hosted on a website that initially – and falsely – claimed it was Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary.
“This was a brazen attempt to mislead audiences and distract from the urgent questions raised by NAZA.”
As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.
Averbuch is the founder of an organisation that says it conducts “advocacy warfare”, including through the publication of scripts to help influencers criticise Abraham and Szor’s critically acclaimed previous film, No Other Land, which documents the destruction of the Palestinian village Masafer Yatta. The two Palestinian co-directors of No Other Land, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, have been harassed or detained by the Israeli military since the film won an Oscar in 2025.
Israeli government officials have scrambled to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.
The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while the military has issued a 10-page response to the film, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
Within a week of NAZA’s premiere, Israel’s ministry of culture had announced a formal investigation into the documentary, calling for Abraham and Szor to be stripped of their citizenship.
Demonstrators gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that the she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.
Spanish film industry members show support for NAZA’s directors at the San Sebastian International film festival on 25 September. Photograph: Ander Gillenea/AFP/Getty On Monday, the far-right Israeli activist Mordechai David announced he was fundraising in order to establish a team that would “chase” Abraham. “We’ll find him,” David said in a video posted to Instagram.
Szor and Abraham addressed the backlash to their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”
At the London film festival on Thursday, one of NAZA’s producers, James Wilson, said Israeli politicians’ “hysterical, vituperative, aggressive backlash” to the documentary had not been anticipated by the team behind it.
Wilson said although Abraham and Szor had “anticipated displeasure … there wasn’t an anticipation of the level of aggression leading to these threats and the rabble-rousing aspect”.
He added: “To have made a film, a documentary film and be threatened by the political elites of your home country, with charges of treason and defamation … it’s been very difficult and stressful and horrible and scary for them.
“I try to look at the overwhelmingly positive reaction to the film in the majority of the world.”

EU lawmakers reject China’s pressure on Taiwan - Taipei Times
The European Parliament on Wednesday adopted a recommendation on EU-China political relations that rejected China’s efforts to restrict Taiwan’s participation in international organizations and exchanges.
The recommendation, addressed to the European Council, the European Commission and EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas, includes several references to EU-Taiwan relations and expresses support for closer ties, saying they would bring positive benefits and have strategic importance.
Describing Taiwan as a valuable partner in trade and technology, the European Parliament said it “rejects China’s attempts to coerce international organizations, third countries and other actors into restricting Taiwan’s international participation and contacts.”
Members of the European Parliament attend a vote during a plenary session at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Wednesday.
It mentions as an example Chinese pressure over Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim’s (蕭美琴) participation in the European Conference of Ventotene for Freedom and Democracy organized by the European Parliament last month.
It also expresses “the EU’s strong disapproval of China’s transnational repression activities,” such as its investigation into Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) under a 2024 judiciary guideline accusing him of launching the “pro-independence separatist organization” Kuma Academy.
The Kuma Academy is a nonprofit dedicated to training civilians on the basics of civil defense.
The recommendation reaffirms that the EU’s “one China” policy guides its policy toward Taiwan and stresses that the EU has never endorsed China’s “one China” principle, the recommendation says.
It also opposes any unilateral attempt to change the “status quo” by force or coercion, or any provocation or any change against the will of Taiwanese.
The recommendation calls for the EU and its member states to work with other democratic partners in the region on closer security coordination, including a continuous naval presence and joint exercises, to reinforce regional stability.
It also calls on the European Commission to fulfill its pledge to parliament to work toward deterring China from provoking or escalating tensions with Taiwan.
At the same time, the commission should continue to develop EU-Taiwan relations in various areas under the EU’s longstanding “one China” policy and encourage dialogue and constructive engagement across the Taiwan Strait, it said.
The recommendation also calls on the UN to reject Chinese demands and grant Republic of China passport holders, including tourists, journalists, non-governmental organization workers and political activists, access to tours and events at the UN.
The European Parliament also opposes what it describes as China’s distortion of UN Resolution 2758 to support its claims over Taiwan’s territory and sovereignty.
UN Resolution 2758 does not mention Taiwan and addresses only the issue of China’s UN representation. Beijing interprets the resolution as giving it the right to represent Taiwan.
The recommendation also stresses the importance of deepening economic and technological cooperation with Taiwan in areas such as semiconductors and cybersecurity to strengthen Europe’s resilience and protect critical supply chains.
It calls for the EU to begin preparations without delay for negotiations on a bilateral investment agreement or another arrangement, such as a memorandum of understanding on critical supply chains, with Taiwan.

Share ‘New tactic’: Russia expands deadly attacks on Ukraine’s transport system on social media
Russian glide bomb hits buses in Ukraine's Kramatorsk, killing at least 30
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian glide bomb struck two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian town of Kramatorsk on Thursday morning, killing at least 30 people and wounding 18, regional authorities said.
Ukrainian officials said the attack was deliberate. When dropped from planes on the Russian side of the front line, such bombs can glide to fixed coordinates on the ground, in this case, a street in the town that lies about 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) from the front line.

“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” regional administration head Vadym Filashkin wrote on Telegram. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill the maximum number of people.”
“Russia consciously disregards all conceivable rules of warfare and norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians,” he wrote.
Filashkin ordered the suspension of the movement of all public transportation in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk as Russia intensifies attacks, paralysing Ukraine’s transport infrastructure, from trains and minibuses to gas stations, bridges, seaports and freight ships.
“This is a new Russian tactic,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “They used to focus on depriving Ukraine of power, on switching off electricity and heating; now their task is also to immobilise the infrastructure, create a transportation collapse.”
“Unfortunately, Russia’s tactic has a certain effect with their strikes on railroads, gas stations,” he said. “They coerce to peace on their conditions.
“They also strike the public psychologically, disrupt the usual lifestyle in general.”
The wreckage of a bus following a Russian missile strike in the eastern city of Kramatorsk, Ukraine [Maria Senovilla/EPA] Throughout the war, Russia has denied it targets Ukrainian civilians, a statement that means little to Ukrainians. During the first eight months of 2026, 15,280 civilians were killed or injured, according to the United Nations – a toll that is 55 percent higher than during the same period in 2025.
With no civilian planes in the sky since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, trains, buses and trucks have become a lifeline for Ukrainian civilians and businesses, as well as for transporting military and humanitarian supplies.
Trains handle almost two-thirds of Ukraine’s freight volumes, including the export of steel slabs, grains and vegetable oils that keep the economy afloat.
At least 521 locomotives have been hit by drones and shelling since 2022, three-fifths this year alone, Ukrzaliznytsia, the state-run railway monopoly, said in late September.
Some locomotives were struck while in motion, and drones have occasionally hit passenger carriages, causing fires, deaths and injuries.
The largest such attack killed five passengers in January in the northeastern Kharkiv region, an act of “terrorism” that was “not militarily justified”, said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Hitting moving trains and buses has become possible because a new generation of Russian drones are no longer the slow, unmanned aircraft that can be jammed electronically or shot down with a machinegun or even an assault rifle.
Jet-powered, with bigger payloads, they are piloted by human operators who use a wireless mesh network, in which each drone serves as a relay node.
“They’re operated manually. The Russians improved their comms,” Andriy Pronin, one of the pioneers of drone warfare in Ukraine, told Al Jazeera.
Occasionally, the signal reaches the drones through a modem on the ground, on a rooftop or even inside somebody’s apartment – switched on by Ukrainians recruited by Russian intelligence, he said.
Locating the modems before attacks is “complicated, but doable”, Pronin said.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, prosecutors and officials, hundreds of recruits, including teenagers, have been offered money via Telegram. They often did not realise the consequences of their actions and have been arrested and convicted.
The video feed and geolocation are often backed by smuggled Ukrainian SIM cards or signals from mobile phone providers in neighbouring, pro-Moscow Belarus, officials believe. These drones can now get almost anywhere in Ukraine, including once-safe western regions.
A train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson crossed into Poland on September 14, just 30 minutes before a Russian drone struck another passenger train’s locomotive at Yahodyn train station in western Ukraine. Former CIA chief David Petraeus was on a nearby train and reportedly described the attack as “terrifying” and “the act of a truly barbaric leader”.
When a daytime Russian drone attack began on September 23, Alyna realised that her workplace was in the most vulnerable place in Kyiv’s central railway station.
She works in a cafeteria located almost in the middle of a massive overpass that stretches above 14 main tracks between the station’s main buildings.
The howling air raid siren and the booms of exploding jet-powered kamikaze drones sent the 24-year-old Kyiv resident scurrying down the stairs and farther on to the subway station.
The drones hit a nearby market, sending black plumes of smoke into the sky and burning to the ground the rotund, modernist building known as the Puck.
“Everything was whistling and rattling above me,” Alyna told Al Jazeera just after another air raid alert ended and passengers began re-entering the station. She withheld her last name for security purposes.
Minutes after the conversation, one more air raid siren forced the passengers out of the railway station, and a drone hit by an interceptor turned into a black cloud in the sky a couple of kilometres east of the building.
The attacks are not limited to trains – Russian drones target petrol stations, buses and minibuses, and seaports, paralysing Ukraine’s exports of grain, vegetable oils and steel.
“You go to a minibus and can hear how [drones] buzz right next to it,” Tetiana Melikhova, a university professor in Zaporizhzhia, a southeastern city with a pre-war population of 720,000, told Al Jazeera.
Her 18-year-old student, Tetiana Bubynets , and two other civilians aged 31 and 48 were killed by an AI-driven drone that was programmed to strike a petrol station on July 6.

OpenAI told investors that it hit roughly $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September, CNBC confirmed, lower than the the $68 billion figure that was widely reported late last month. A person familiar with the matter said the $68 billion figure included gross revenue from OpenAI's partners, which helps investors make a more direct comparison with its chief rival, Anthropic .
The Financial Times was first to report the $50 billion figure.
OpenAI shared an update about its finances in an investor presentation, said the person, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the numbers. In addition to the $50 billion in annualized revenue, OpenAI touted 77% total run rate growth during its third quarter, as well as 107% run rate growth for its enterprise business during the same period, the person said.

Why are gas prices still high even as traffic improves in the Strait of Hormuz?
Gas prices stand above $4.30, marking an increase of 46% from pre-war levels.
Oil exports from the Middle East have improved substantially in recent weeks, according to a post on X from private tracking firm Kpler, but gas prices still stand above $4.30, and diesel prices remain close to an all-time high.
The supply of oil from the Gulf, excluding Iran, has returned to where it stood before the Iran war, Kpler said last week. Roughly four of every 10 barrels of crude now exit the region without going through the Strait of Hormuz , an adjustment in the oil supply chain, Kpler added.
At the same time, Kpler said on Wednesday, tanker traffic in the strait has improved significantly from a low point earlier in the war, bolstering exports from the region.
It depends on who you ask: Trump and Vance offer slightly different takes on the economy
The apparent disconnect between a recovery in oil supply and stubborn fuel prices has drawn attention from analysts. The dynamics behind gas prices have garnered added urgency as the United States hurtles toward midterm elections in less than a month.
"Aren't we all trying to figure that out?" Dominic Pappalardo, chief multi-asset strategist at Morningstar Wealth, told ABC News.
Analysts who spoke to ABC News attributed persistently high gas prices to lingering disruption in the region, which has forced firms to take up costly means of transporting crude and pass along those expenses to retailers.
Oil traders, meanwhile, question the staying power of newfound Middle Eastern supply, keeping crude prices higher than the level of oil flow may otherwise suggest, they said. Investors fear a potential resumption of large-scale fighting in the strait or attacks on oil infrastructure in the region, some analysts said.
Plus, analysts added, gas prices typically drop at a delayed pace in response to any reduction in oil prices, in part because it takes time for retailers to sell through refined product purchased while oil prices were at higher levels.
"When prices are fluctuating, gas stations want to protect their profit margin. They don't want to cut prices too quickly," Christopher Tang, a professor of supply chain management at the University of California, told ABC News.
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, Oct, 6, 2026.
The U.S. -- the world's largest oil producer -- imports a small amount of crude from the Middle East. Since oil and gas are sold on a global market, however, the shortage has sent prices rising for everyone, including U.S. drivers.
A large-scale U.S.-Israeli attack in the winter prompted Iran's closure of the strait, resulting in the largest oil supply shock ever recorded. Oil prices surged, catapulting inflation to its highest level since 2023.
Alternative trade routes in the region helped ease the fallout, but exports remained well below pre-war levels until recently.

To be sure, oil prices have dropped in recent weeks as supply blockages have eased. The West Texas Intermediate futures price, the benchmark index for U.S. trading, stands at about $92. That figure amounts to a roughly 9% drop since Sept. 15. The price, however, remains more than 40% higher than pre-war levels.
Oil prices account for a large share of the price of gasoline and diesel. The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. currently registers at $4.36, marking a decline of about 21 cents over the past month, according to AAA . Still, gas prices stand 46% higher than pre-war levels.
Even though oil supply from the Gulf has mostly recovered, the cost of transporting crude still exceeds pre-war levels, attaching new expenses to the product as it moves through the supply chain to refiners, retailers and ultimately drivers, some analysts said.
Tankers have undertaken ship-to-ship transfers as a means of evading possible attack. The cost-intensive maneuver involves direct transfer of oil from one ship to another while the two are at sea, handing off the crude to a flagged ship that carries less risk. After exiting the strait, for instance, one ship may pass oil to another.
Another source of added cost: Some tanker captains are garnering higher pay as they face increased danger, the Financial Times (FT) reported earlier this week. Some captains are receiving base salaries as high as $100,000 a month, as well as a $50,000 bonus for each trip, the outlet found. Typically, regular pay for captains is $15,000 per month, according to the FT.
"Transportation costs are still quite high. Bear in mind, the war is still going on," Tang said. "The crude oil is moving, but the price is much higher than before the attack on Iran."
The persistence of high gas prices traces in part to uncertainty about the path forward for the Iran war, some analysts said.
An alternative trade route in the region, Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline , underscores jitters felt in oil markets.

The pipeline temporarily closed last month, however, after an attack carried out by Iran-aligned Houthi militants. Oil exports through the pipeline were restored to 5.8 million barrels a day earlier this week, Reuters reported.
Still, some analysts said, concern remains about potential Houthi attacks on the pipeline or tankers in the nearby Bab el-Mandeb Strait , which feeds into the Red Sea.

items.title: More rate hikes are coming, says Fed's Waller - Mortgage Professional America
items.summary: More rate hikes are coming, says Fed's Waller  Mortgage Professional America
items.content:
Fed governor sees more central bank moves ahead as inflation holds above 2%, with no fixed schedule for tightening
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller signaled Thursday that the September rate increase is not the ceiling of this tightening cycle, calling for additional hikes while keeping the calendar open to data.
Addressing the Central Bank of Türkiye's Istanbul Economic Forum , Waller said, "If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal. But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
What's behind the Federal Reserve's September hike?
Three compounding forces drove Waller's September vote:
a Middle East conflict projected to keep oil prices elevated through at least 2027
an artificial intelligence (AI) buildout inflating high-tech consumer prices, and
renewed tariff threats from continued trade disputes
Core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation stood at 3% year-over-year and 0.25% monthly as of August, well above the Fed's 2% target.
On recession risk, Waller was unequivocal. "With evidence that economic activity is strengthening in the second half of this year, I am not greatly concerned that tighter monetary policy threatens a damaging slowdown in the economy," he said.
"But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation."
Where are mortgage rates headed next? Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality, says the base case still points to lower mortgage rates over time, but inflation, bond yields, and geopolitical uncertainty continue to create significant volatility. https://t.co/FHN37YJIKP
— Mortgage Professional America Magazine (@MPAMagazineUS) October 8, 2026
Waller defended the Fed's practice of signal-based communication as a middle ground between silence and binding commitments.
"Policymakers could signal where they are likely headed while acknowledging that there is no fixed final destination — except for the achievement of price stability and maximum employment," he said.
"This signaling helps to anchor the path of short-term interest rates but provides flexibility in adjusting rate hikes based on incoming data."
Futures markets priced an 85% probability of at least one hike before December.
For brokers managing client conversations, Melissa Cohn, regional vice president at William Raveis Mortgage and a 44-year industry veteran, offered a counterintuitive read in a Mortgage Professional America analysis on why mortgage rates could fall as the Fed hikes .
"Remember: at the beginning of the last rate-cutting cycle, mortgage rates actually went up when the Fed was cutting rates. I think there's a very good reason mortgage rates could go down if the Fed actually does raise rates," she explained.

Fed holds interest rates steady as inflation hits 3-year high
Futures markets overwhelmingly expected the Fed to keep rates unchanged.
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday as the economy weathers its highest inflation in three years.
The announcement marked the first decision on interest rates rates since Trump nominee Kevin Warsh took the helm as Fed chair.
Speaking at a press conference, Warsh voiced a commitment to bring inflation down to the Fed's desired level of 2%. The annual pace of price increases currently registers at more than twice that target rate.
"Persistently high prices are a burden for the American people," Warsh told reporters in Washington, D.C. "This committee will deliver price stability."
All 12 members of the FOMC voted to hold interest rates steady, meaning Warsh and his predecessor, former Fed Chair Jerome Powell, agreed on the rate decision.
Nine members indicated they expect to raise interest rates by the end of the year, marking a significant change in sentiment from a previous projection issued three months earlier.
Iran live updates: Trump, Vance were both signatories on MOU
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), a 12-member policymaking body at the Fed, issued a statement describing inflation as "elevated."
The current level of inflation in part reflects "supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy," the FOMC said.
The policy move also arrived at a moment of flux for the nation’s economy, just days after an agreement between the United States and Iran offered hope for some price relief.
The U.S.-Iran accord, set to be formally signed on Friday, came as gasoline prices fell below $4 a gallon for the first time since March. Still, fuel costs stand well above pre-war levels, and an array of grocery prices remain elevated.
In recent weeks, odds have risen for a potential interest rate hike by the end of 2026, according to the CME FedWatch Tool, which grants a roughly four in 10 chance of a quarter-point increase in December.
The shift in expectations came after a stronger-than-expected jobs report earlier this month showed robust hiring in May. In theory, a resilient labor market could afford central bankers leeway to raise interest rates in an effort to dial back inflation, since elevated borrowing costs risk a hiring slowdown.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh delivers a speech on the day of his swearing-in ceremony, in the East Room of the White House in Washington, May 22, 2026.
The Middle East conflict prompted the Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz , a maritime trading route that facilitates the transport of about one-fifth of global oil supply. The standoff triggered one of the largest oil shocks ever recorded, sending gasoline prices surging.
On Monday, President Donald Trump announced a U.S.-Iran deal that included plans to reopen the strait. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi confirmed the deal had been finalized and said it would be signed in Switzerland on Friday. Oil prices fell to their lowest level since March.
The benchmark rate stands at a level between 3.5% and 3.75%. That figure marks a significant drop from a recent peak attained in 2023, but borrowing costs remain well above a 0% rate established at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The rate decision is the first major policy move overseen by Warsh. During his term as a Fed governor in the late 2000s and early 2010s, Warsh gained a reputation as an interest-rate "hawk," meaning he generally preferred higher interest rates as a means of ensuring low and stable inflation.
Last year, Warsh voiced support for lower interest rates. At his Senate confirmation hearing in April, Warsh emphasized the threat posed by elevated inflation.
"When inflation surges -- as it has done in recent years -- grievous harm is done to our citizens, especially to the least well-off," Warsh said.
Bucking typical norms, Powell casted a vote on interest rates as a member of the Fed's policymaking board.

Powell said he would stay on at the central bank's board of governors after his term as chair expired as an investigation into the Fed's office renovation continues.
The Department of Justice moved to drop a criminal probe into Powell in April, calling on the Fed's inspector general to carry out the investigation into cost overruns tied to the renovation. Powell will remain on the Fed's board for an indeterminate length of time, he said last month.
The criminal investigation into Powell focused on alleged false testimony to Congress about an office renovation. Powell, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, has rebuked the probe as a politically motivated effort to influence interest-rate policy. Trump denied any involvement in the criminal investigation.

items.title: Florida judge allows lawsuit against Shah of Iran’s alleged ‘chief torturer’ to move forward
items.summary: Parviz Sabeti denies allegations he led Savak intelligence agency under shah and directed torture of thousandsThe alleged “chief torturer” for the deposed Shah of Iran is a step closer to trial for human rights abuses after a Florida federal judge rejected his demand to halt a lawsuit brought by three former political prisoners.Parviz Sabeti, who was reported <
items.content:
Parviz Sabeti in an undated picture. Photograph: Alamy
Parviz Sabeti in an undated picture. Photograph: Alamy
Florida judge allows lawsuit against Shah of Iran’s alleged ‘chief torturer’ to move forward
Parviz Sabeti denies allegations he led Savak intelligence agency under shah and directed torture of thousands
The alleged “chief torturer” for the deposed Shah of Iran is a step closer to trial for human rights abuses after a Florida federal judge rejected his demand to halt a lawsuit brought by three former political prisoners.
Parviz Sabeti, who was reported last year to have lived in a quiet upscale central Florida community, is accused of being the former head of Savak, the shah’s secret police and intelligence agency. The plaintiffs say they discovered his whereabouts only after a photo of Sabeti at a 2023 protest against the Iranian government was posted on social media by his daughter.
He could now be made to answer as early as next year to civil claims under the Torture Victim Protection Act (TVPA) that he directed and took part in the detention and torture of thousands of the shah’s political opponents in jails in Tehran and elsewhere until the Islamic revolution swept the regime from power in 1979.
‘A return to prison is always looming’: Iran’s Nobel laureate recounts torture in jail and hopes for the future
Sabeti has denied allegations that that he was personally involved or that Savak tortured detainees, and claimed that he “ always opposed torture ”.
Tuesday’s sealed order by the district court judge Gregory A Presnell rejected Sabeti’s argument that a statute of limitations on the allegations should be strictly enforced and a summary judgment issued in his favor.
In August 2025, Presnell rejected a motion by Sabeti’s lawyers to dismiss the case outright, ordering the parties to conduct discovery on whether the TVPA claim was time-barred, and said he would listen to arguments about why the deadline should not be extended.
Sabeti’s lawyers dispute that he was difficult to find and sue before 2023, filing dozens of documents which they said proved he had lived openly in Florida under his real name, including property records, media articles, and a photograph of Sabeti with George HW Bush and his son Jeb Bush, a former governor of Florida.
In May, attorneys for the three Iranian plaintiffs filed a response presenting dozens of documents and articles of their own to try to bolster their argument that there were extraordinary circumstances in the case that warranted an extension of time to bring the claim.
They included the Guardian’s September 2025 story that chronicled Sabeti’s departure from Iran and his low-profile new life in Florida, where the lawsuit asserts he “has spent the last four decades out of the public eye, concealing his whereabouts and identity”.
As the Guardian reported last year, Sabeti was identified as a fiercely loyal ally of the shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, in a secret analysis by the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) written in 1978, which was not released until 2018.
According to the complaint, he was “widely recognized as one of the most powerful and feared men in the shah’s regime … with the authority to apprehend, interrogate and prosecute opponents throughout the country”.
The plaintiffs, Iranian men living in California aged 68 to 85, claim they were among thousands of people rounded up as perceived opponents of the shah by Savak , Iran’s notoriously brutal internal security and intelligence agency, and subjected to abuses at Sabeti’s personal direction.
Among their claims made under the TVPA are that their captors used rape, electric shocks, near-drownings and forced nail extraction against political prisoners. They say they were abducted by Savak in Tehran, beaten into giving false confessions and served prison time.
The lawsuit details the alleged use of a torture device nicknamed Apollo, an electric chair named after the early US space program, which featured a metal helmet that amplified victims’ screams into their own ears.
Sabeti has previously insisted he was not involved in the detention, torture or execution of prisoners. A 2023 report on the website of the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran, a dissident group, cited an interview Sabeti gave to the Persian channel Manoto in which he characterized his government employment as clerical work.
Court papers list seven attorneys for Sabeti. None replied to the Guardian’s request for comment by the time of publication.
Claret Vargas, senior staff attorney for the Center for Justice and Accountability, an advocacy group representing the three Iranian plaintiffs, welcomed Presnell’s ruling, which she said allows the case to move forward towards discovery on the TVPA allegations against Sabeti. The court previously dismissed the state law claims.
“I’m very glad that our clients will be able to pursue justice after all these years, and everybody deserves justice for torture regardless of who was in charge, or the regime that tortured them,” she said.
“Perpetrators of torture should not escape accountability simply because the survivors were forced to live with fear for decades.
“We don’t yet know the specific legal basis for the court’s decision, but it’s a really important milestone for our clients to be able to bring forth this case and really address [their allegations].”
Donald Trump’s war in Iran has brought new scrutiny of the resilience of the country’s hardline Islamic regime, and the strength of the opposition to it among a sizable Iranian expat community in the US.
Washington DC-based Reza Pahlavi, the former shah’s son, has positioned himself as a possible new leader if the current regime falls, although questions remain over his level of popular support.
In June, Pahlavi, 65, was forced to distance himself from far-right supporters who flew banners and wore shirts with the Savak emblem at rallies.
Divisions between various opposition groups of Iranians in the US were highlighted by the killing in Canada earlier this year of the Iranian activist Masood Masjoody , a critic of the US-led war and the campaign to install Pahlavi as the country’s next leader.
According to the Associated Press, Masjoody’s sudden disappearance in February was followed by a threatening post on X in Farsi directed at other activists by a since-deleted account named for Savak.

items.content:
Microsoft starts taking preorders for $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra
Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra contains an Nvidia chip that can run large AI models without generating cloud bills.
The device contains a magnetic USB-C port similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector.
Microsoft also said that Meta will introduce its Muse AI agent for Windows.
Microsoft said its new laptop containing an Nvidia AI chip will start at $2,599, as the software maker tries to bring more artificial intelligence capabilities to its consumer devices.
The Surface Laptop Ultra is now available on preorder and will begin shipping on Oct. 16, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president of Windows and devices, said at a company event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The computer has the world's first magnetic USB-C port, similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector, along with two other standard USB-C ports, Microsoft said in a blog post .
While Microsoft Windows is the most popular operating system for PCs, the company isn't among the top six PC vendors in terms of unit shipments, according to an estimate from researcher Gartner. As the AI boom matures and chip technology advances, tech giants including Microsoft, Apple and Google are aiming to allow users to run more AI workloads from their devices rather than relying on the cloud.
Users can install and run a variety of models on the new laptop without having to worry about racking up high monthly bills. Microsoft first talked about the Surface Laptop Ultra in May, but is just now providing specifics.
"Microsoft might get me back to Windows," Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies, wrote on X after the announcement.
Davuluri also said that Meta will introduce a version of its popular Muse AI agent for Windows, capitalizing on the surging popularity of the personal agent, which has jumped to the top of Apple's App store, surpassing ChatGPT.
Microsoft is still trying to solidify its role as a key player in AI. The company offers its own AI models, but they're less popular than leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic and aren't at the forefront in terms of performance, according to one benchmark . Developers are more likely to have used alternatives, according to a recent survey .
This isn't the first time Microsoft has sought to use the AI boom as a way to boost sales of its devices.
In 2024, the company introduced the Copilot+ PC standard, requiring the inclusion of neural processing units that ensure a minimum level of AI performance, along with compliant Surface computers. But Microsoft has since "simplified product naming to lead with the Surface brand, while continuing to deliver premium hardware and hybrid AI experiences," a spokesperson said.
Microsoft Windows Surface Laptop Ultra and Surface RTX Spark Dev Box
The new device sports a 15-inch display and weighs 4.4 pounds. It can contain up to 128 gigabytes of unified memory and supply up to one petaflop of computing power. The Blackwell RTX Spark GPU inside the computer has as much processing power as Nvidia's DGX-1 data center server from 2016, which cost $250 million, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at Wednesday's event.
A presenter showed how apps on the Surface Laptop Ultra can route some AI coding requests run on the computer's local GPU, displaying a green leaf icon, and others to the cloud. Through Windows 11, developers can confine coding agents to Microsoft Execution Containers that will prevent unwanted system access.
Microsoft is updating its Windows 11 device setup experience to help people get started quickly with open-source OpenClaw AI agent software.
Microsoft has been releasing its own computers since 2012, and CEO Satya Nadella indicated on Tuesday that the company's position in the market is evolving.
"I think today is the day we'll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours two years from now, five years from now, 10 years from now," Nadella said at the event. "That classic edge that distributed computing will always remain distributed will be more true."

items.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
items.summary: Pioneering computer scientist led the development of the software for Nasa's Apollo mission and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
items.content:
Figure caption, Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom
The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.
Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".
Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.
"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.
It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.
But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
Image caption, Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969
In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel.
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958.
She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
"We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media.
"Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said.

items.title: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
items.summary: Students' blockades and marches spring from real grievances – and from France's habit of settling policy on the street.
items.content:
Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.
The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested.
The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds.
"Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.
There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 19:00, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2.
France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.
The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.
Figure caption, Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas on Tuesday
Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries?
According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools.
Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay.
Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries.
The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system.
In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too.
And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
Image caption, About 500 people were arrested during Tuesday's unrest
The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks.
Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law.
To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else.
In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées.
In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff.
On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994.
Figure caption, Why has France suspended the use of stun grenades on protesters?
Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment.
The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence.
French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending.
In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people.
On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BFMTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement.
Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon.
Image caption, Lecornu will find it difficult to open the purse strings
The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time.
His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament.
But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung.
Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give.
